\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a way to measure complex tastes---cases where what people like, do, and praise do not line up---using data that record preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural items. The approach applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) method, and lets us ask concrete questions about complex tastes: Do preference, engagement, and evaluation contribute equally to the structure that emerges? Do some dimensions of complex taste hang together more than others? The method also captures a duality: individuals vary in how much their own tastes are complex, and genres vary in how much they attract complex tastes from the people who encounter them. I demonstrate the approach using data on Americans' tastes in twenty musical genres, collected around 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}: a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}: actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}: judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree: what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not: the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per aspect of taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory raises directly: How strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And where, geometrically, do complex tastes live?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data}

I use the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi}, a national sample of $N = 2{,}276$ American adults surveyed around 2012. For each of twenty musical genres, the survey measures how much a respondent likes the genre, whether they consume it, and how they perceive the social characteristics of its typical fans. Listwise deletion of the $17$ cases missing data on any of the $60$ analysis variables leaves an analytic sample of $N = 2{,}259$ respondents.

\subsection{Measures: Three Aspects of Taste for Twenty Genres}

Each genre contributes three binary indicators, one per aspect, for $20 \times 3 = 60$ variables organized into three blocks of twenty. \textit{Preference} comes from a four-point liking scale (like; dislike; neither like nor dislike; not familiar); a genre is coded $1$ if the respondent likes it and $0$ otherwise, treating unfamiliarity as non-liking on the reasoning that an affective response requires knowing the object. \textit{Consumption} (engagement) is whether the respondent checked having listened to the genre in the past month ($1 = $ listened, $0 = $ otherwise). \textit{Evaluation} comes from a check-all-that-apply list of the social characteristics respondents attribute to a genre's ``typical fan,'' so the categories are not mutually exclusive---a respondent can indicate both that the typical fan is a college graduate and that they did not attend college, or that they are both working class and upper class. A genre is coded $1$ if the respondent attributed \emph{unambiguously} high status to its typical fans---a college graduate without also indicating no college, \emph{or} middle or upper class without also indicating working or lower class---and $0$ otherwise.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} reports how often respondents are coded $1$ on each indicator. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are positive on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding---it requires an uncontested high-status signal in at least one domain---so evaluation is the least frequently affirmed aspect: respondents grant a genre's fans unambiguous high status less readily than they like the genre or listen to it.

\section{Analytic Strategy}

Multiple Factor Analysis \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa} is built for data structures like this one, namely, a set of individuals described by several blocks of variables, with the goal of a common representation that treats the blocks---here, the three aspects of complex tastes---as comparable without letting any one dominate from the outset. The MFA literature calls these variable sets ``groups'' \citep{pages2014mfa}; we call them \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning. In the GDA tradition that also includes Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), the values a categorical variable can take---here \emph{yes} and \emph{no}---are called its \emph{modalities} \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44}; we simply call them \emph{categories}.

\subsection{Constructing the Global Complex Taste Space}

The global MFA analysis starts from a table with one row per individual and sixty columns---twenty genres times three aspects---recording each individual's preferences, consumption, and evaluations. Cell $ijk$, for row $i$, column $j$ (genre), and aspect $k$, equals 1 if individual $i$ likes, consumes, or highly evaluates genre $j$. The analysis proceeds in two steps. First, we run a separate MCA on each of the three individual-by-genre tables (20 columns apiece), one per aspect. Second, we combine the three analyses into a single global analysis spanning all sixty columns, weighting each block by the inverse of its first eigenvalue---obtained from the separate MCA---so all three aspects contribute comparably, regardless of the prominence of the first dimension in the separate analysis. We call the resulting global structure the ``complex taste space.''\footnote{As a robustness check, we re-estimated the same MFA with each block analyzed by a scaled PCA of the binary indicators instead of MCA; the substantive results hold up. The eigenvalues agree to two decimals ($1.504$, $1.188$, and $0.997$ versus $1.509$, $1.178$, and $0.982$ on the first three dimensions); the RV structure is unchanged (preference--consumption $0.32$; evaluation--preference and evaluation--consumption $0.01$ and $0.01$); individual coordinates correlate at $0.98$, $0.97$, and $0.84$ across the first three dimensions (up to sign), and the aspect-disagreement scores at $0.96$, $0.89$, and $0.77$; the aspect-disagreement shares of projected partial inertia are $56\%$, $53\%$, and $61\%$, against $56\%$, $52\%$, and $63\%$ in the MCA version. The one real difference concerns rare categories: MCA gives them proportionally more weight, stretching out the most distinctive affirmations---a feature here, since the rare affirmations carry the theoretical interest.}

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy of Aspects of Complex Tastes}

MFA provides concrete quantities that answer the measurement questions complex tastes raise. The first question is whether the three aspects are empirically redundant or partially independent. Partial independence is what justifies studying complex tastes in the first place. If preferences carried the same information as consumption or evaluation, studying simple tastes based on preferences alone would do, however elegant the abstract complex-taste argument. The comparison relies on the geometry each aspect imposes on the individuals; an aspect's twenty indicators generate a cloud of the same $N$ respondents, and that cloud is fully described by the distances between them---who stands near whom depends on which aspect is consulted (e.g., individuals who like the same genres are close in genre space and individuals who consume the same genres are close in the consumption space).

The \textit{RV coefficient} between two blocks of variables (here, two aspects) compresses the similarity of their two inter-individual distance structures into a single number, the multivariate analog of a squared correlation, running from 0 to 1. RV is 0 exactly when every indicator of one aspect is unrelated to every indicator of the other, and two respondents who are close together in one cloud are no more likely to be close in the other than two respondents chosen at random (e.g., a person's preferences are unrelated to the genres they consider high status). RV is 1 when the two clouds have exactly the same shape, so the distance between any pair of respondents in one cloud is a fixed multiple of their distance in the other; the aspects agree completely about who resembles whom and differ only in how far apart they spread the respondents (e.g., a person's engagements are perfectly predictable from their preferences). If preference, engagement, and evaluation induced similar structures (high RV coefficients between them), any one could stand in for the others, and a person's tastes could be captured by simple tastes alone. Small RV coefficients mean the opposite. Each aspect carries information the others lack, so no single aspect can speak for a person's tastes. Taste profiles whose aspects do not line up---complex tastes---then become an empirical reality rather than a conceptual possibility.\footnote{For each block $h$, let $\mathbf{S}_h$ be the block's configuration matrix: the matrix of weighted cross-products between respondents induced by its twenty indicators, $\mathbf{S}_h = \mathbf{Z}_h \mathbf{W}_h \mathbf{Z}_h'$, where $\mathbf{Z}_h$ is the centered indicator matrix and $\mathbf{W}_h$ holds the MCA column weights. The $(i,i')$ entry of $\mathbf{S}_h$ is large when respondents $i$ and $i'$ answer alike on that aspect's twenty genres, and the configuration matrix and the matrix of squared interindividual distances carry the same information, so comparing configurations is comparing distance structures. The RV coefficient between blocks $h$ and $k$ is $\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}$: the cosine between the two configurations, treated as vectors of pairwise respondent similarities. When each block contains a single variable, RV reduces to the squared Pearson correlation.}

\subsection{Interpretation of Complex Taste Space Dimensions}

The second question is whether each aspect actually contributes to the common representation MFA builds, which matters for interpreting the global complex taste space. The \textit{$Lg$ coefficient} measures the strength of the link between a block of variables and the global structure, that is, how much of the block's own geometry shows up in the global space.\footnote{$Lg(h,k)$ is the inner product between the configurations that forms the numerator of the RV coefficient, without RV's normalizations: with respondents carrying equal weight, $Lg(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k)/N^2$, where the configuration matrices carry the MCA column weights, which absorb the balancing weights. $Lg$ is symmetric in its arguments, and $Lg(h,h)$ is the aspect's overall inertia in the global metric: the sum of the squared eigenvalues of its separate analysis. $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ takes the compromise configuration as the second argument, and normalizes the global analysis as a block by its first eigenvalue, $\lambda_1$.} Where RV asks only whether two aspects structure respondents similarly, discarding how much structure they share, $Lg$ counts the shared structure itself, or the ``number of common dimensions,'' each ``weighted'' by its inertia \citep[p.~137]{pages2014mfa}. We therefore use RV to compare the aspects with one another and $Lg$ to gauge each aspect's link to the global complex taste space. $Lg$ assigns each aspect a single number---it asks about the aspect's participation in the compromise as a whole, not about any one dimension of it---and because it's on an absolute scale, it can be compared across aspects and against the common structure. The balancing weights guarantee equal influence for the three aspects going in, not equal presence in the result. In principle, an aspect with a much weaker internal structure could end up present in name only in the global structure. $Lg$ thus tells us whether each aspect leaves a detectable imprint on the complex taste space, or whether the compromise quietly drops one in favor of the other two.

\subsection{Composition of Complex Taste Space Dimensions}

The third question is which aspects organize each dimension of the shared space. The \textit{aspect contributions}---called \emph{group contributions} in the MFA literature---apportion the variance of each dimension of the common representation among the three aspects. This is a different quantity from $Lg$. $Lg$ assigns each aspect one number, while the contributions assign each dimension one decomposition across aspects. The contributions reveal whether preference, engagement, and evaluation jointly constitute the axes of the taste space, or whether a dimension is instead dominated by, say, consumption at the expense of the other two. This matters for complex tastes because a dimension dominated by a single aspect---one organized by what respondents praise rather than by what they prefer or consume---is exactly where the aspects can come apart, and so where complex tastes should show up.\footnote{Formally, the contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is $\mathrm{ctr}(h,s) = \sum_{j \in h} w_j f_{js}^2 / \lambda_s$: the sum over the aspect's twenty variables of their weighted squared coordinates on the dimension, divided by the dimension's eigenvalue $\lambda_s$; the three aspects' contributions sum to $100\%$ on every dimension.}

\subsection{Measuring Complex Taste at the Individual Level}

MFA's block structure also gives us the machinery to measure individual complex tastes directly in the geometry of the space. In the combined representation, each individual $i$ has $H$ \emph{partial points}---one per aspect, so $H = 3$ here---whose average is the individual's global point. For a given dimension $s$, individual $i$'s projected partial inertia decomposes exactly as
\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}
where $H$ is the number of aspects (three here), $h = 1, \dots, H$ indexes them, $F_s(i)$ is the individual's global coordinate, and $F_{sh}(i)$ is their partial coordinate from aspect $h$. The first term locates the individual in the common space; the second, $W_s(i)$, measures how spread out the aspect-specific points are around that common position. It is zero when the three aspects place the individual identically---the geometry of a simple taste---and grows as the aspects disagree more. Read strictly, $W_s(i)$ is the individual's \emph{aspect-disagreement} on dimension $s$: how much the person's position on that dimension depends on which aspect of taste we consult. We interpret that disagreement as complex taste because a profile whose aspects place the person in different locations cannot be summarized by any single taste position.

The squared pairwise distances between partial points break $W_s(i)$ down further, into disagreement between specific pairs of aspects: $d^2(i)_{s,\text{pc}}$ for preference--consumption, $d^2(i)_{s,\text{pe}}$ for preference--evaluation, and $d^2(i)_{s,\text{ce}}$ for consumption--evaluation. The three distances sum to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so each pair's share of that sum tells us how much of the disagreement that pair of aspects is responsible for.\footnote{On dimension $s$, the squared distance between the partial points of aspects $h$ and $k$ is the squared difference of their coordinates on that dimension, $d^2_s(h,k) = \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i)\right)^2$. The three pairwise distances sum exactly to $H$ times the aspect-disagreement $W_s(i)$, $\sum_{h<k} d^2_s(h,k) = H \cdot W_s(i)$, which follows from the identity $\sum_{h<k}\left(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i)\right)^2 = H \sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 - \left(\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)\right)^2$ together with $F_s(i) = H^{-1} \sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)$.} This is also the level at which Ma's configurations are defined: each of the six complex configurations is a case of one aspect standing against the other two---evaluation against engagement in the distant praise and the guilty pleasure, consumption against liking and evaluation in the taste pose and the distanced consumption, liking against the other two in the pre-acquired taste and the justified abstention---so the pairwise decomposition speaks Ma's typology, indicating not just how much the aspects disagree but which aspect is standing apart from the others.

Moreover, each partial individual point in complex taste space is itself the sum of its aspect's twenty per-genre contributions---one per genre, determined by which of the genre's two categories the respondent chose. Decomposing $W_s(i)$ into these contributions separates two kinds of taste complexity that otherwise would be mixed up.\footnote{For dimension $s$, genre $g$, and aspect $h$, the contribution is $c_{ighs} = \Delta_{ghs}\,(z_{igh} - p_{gh})$, where $z_{igh}$ is the respondent's binary value, $p_{gh}$ its margin in the sample, and $\Delta_{ghs}$ the difference between the two categories' weighted contributions in the global analysis, scaled by $\sqrt{p_{gh}(1 - p_{gh})}$. The coordinates are exact sums of these contributions: $F_{sh}(i) = H \sum_g c_{ighs}$ and $F_s(i) = \sum_{g,h} c_{ighs}$.} The contribution $c_{ighs}$ carries four subscripts---$i$ for the individual, $g$ for the genre, $h$ for the aspect, and $s$ for the dimension---so once we fix the individual, the genre, and the dimension, the three aspects' contributions can be compared directly. We write $\bar{c}_{igs} = H^{-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H} c_{ighs}$ for the mean of genre $g$'s three contributions on dimension $s$, and $d_{ighs} = c_{ighs} - \bar{c}_{igs}$ for how far aspect $h$'s contribution departs from that mean: positive when aspect $h$ carries individual $i$ further along dimension $s$ in genre $g$ than the three aspects do on average, negative when it carries them less far. In terms of these deviations, the aspect-disagreement score splits exactly into a genre-based part and a cross-genre remainder:
\begin{equation}
W_s(i) \;=\;
\underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} \omega_s(i;g)}_{\text{genre-based complex taste}} \;+\;
\underbrace{2H^2 \sum_{g<g'} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}\, d_{ig'hs}}_{\text{cross-genre coherence}},
\qquad \omega_s(i;g) \;=\; H^2 \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}^2,
\label{eq:genre}
\end{equation}
where $G = 20$ is the number of genres. The first term is the respondent's \emph{genre-based complex taste}: it collects the disagreement that lives inside particular genres, since $\omega_s(i;g)$ is zero when the three aspects place the respondent identically for genre $g$, grows as they disagree about that one genre, and is the geometric expression of holding a complex configuration in that genre---a guilty pleasure, a taste pose, a distant praise. The second term, which we call the \emph{cross-genre coherence} of the aspects, registers whether the aspects' disagreements point the same way across genres: it is large when one pattern---valuation outrunning engagement, or engagement outrunning valuation---repeats across the genre portfolio, and it is negative when the respondent's genre-based complex tastes point in opposite directions across genres and cancel. The aspect-disagreement score therefore aggregates two different phenomena: complex tastes based in specific genres, and a systematic orientation of one aspect against the other two. Equation~\ref{eq:genre} separates them.

Consider two hypothetical respondents: The first holds a single conspicuous complex taste---a guilty pleasure in one genre---while the three aspects agree closely everywhere else; the score is almost entirely genre-based complex taste. The second holds no strong disagreement about any single genre, but the aspects tilt the same way in all twenty---evaluation contributing a little more than engagement in each---so the small per-genre tilts accumulate into a large gap between the evaluation point and the other two; the score is almost entirely coherence. Two respondents can thus reach the same total disagreement from opposite materials. Section~\ref{sec:antinomies} walks a single respondent through all three scores and the genre-level split (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}) once the dimensions of the space have been read.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Overall Structure of the Complex Taste Space}

Table~\ref{tab:eigen} reports the eigenvalue decomposition of the global complex taste space from the MFA. The first dimension ($\lambda_1 = 1.51$) accounts for $9.6\%$ of the variance, the second ($\lambda_2 = 1.18$) for $7.5\%$; the first five dimensions cumulate to $32.5\%$. Percentages this size are typical for categorical GDA of sparse binary indicators, where a large share of the variance is idiosyncratic, genre-by-genre variation.\footnote{We conducted all analyses in \textsf{R} using \textsf{FactoMineR}; scripts reproducing all results are available in the replication materials.}

The category coordinates support a coherent reading of the first three dimensions (Figure~\ref{fig:categories12} and~\ref{fig:categories}). As Figure~\ref{fig:categories12} shows, on the first dimension, the ``yes'' categories of preference and consumption sit on the positive side of the origin---listening to folk ($+1.43$), bluegrass ($+1.34$), reggae ($+1.24$), and opera ($+1.13$) are the most extreme (and rarest) consumption affirmations---while the matching ``no'' categories sit on the negative side. Genre evaluations, by contrast, barely differentiate respondents on this axis: attributing unambiguous high status to a genre's fans ranges only from $+0.03$ (Broadway/show tunes) to $+0.53$ (rap/hip-hop), an order of magnitude less distinctive than the consumption affirmations. Dimension 1 is thus a \emph{general affirmation} axis: a gradient in the overall propensity to like and to listen, running from generalized non-engagement to generalized engagement with the genre system. The rarest categories receive the most extreme scores, as is typical of MCA \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44}; the status attributions save their distinctiveness for the third dimension, to which we return below.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.85\linewidth]{fig-categories12} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored points are the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. Preference and consumption ``yes'' categories array along the positive side of Dimension 1 (general affirmation); the evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread along it, while splitting highbrow (top) from popular (bottom) on Dimension 2.}
\label{fig:categories12}
\end{figure}

As Figure~\ref{fig:categories12} shows, Dimension 2 organizes genres \textit{hierarchically} rather than by aspect. At one pole sit the ``yes'' categories of the consecrated, highbrow end of the genre system (big band $+0.98$, opera $+0.86$, Broadway and show tunes $+0.84$, classical and bluegrass $+0.73$, folk $+0.68$); at the other sit rap/hip-hop ($-0.91$ and $-0.84$ for consumption and preference), indie and alternative rock ($-0.84$), heavy metal ($-0.78$), dance/club ($-0.75$), and reggae ($-0.63$). Dimension 2 is thus a \emph{highbrow--popular} axis that holds within all three aspects at once. The individual factor maps (Figure~\ref{fig:individuals}) give a first look at this axis's social anchoring: respondents are strongly ordered by age, with the youngest cohort toward the popular pole and the oldest toward the highbrow pole (Section~\ref{sec:social}). The map's vertical axis also previews Dimension 3: all twenty ``yes'' categories of the genre evaluations sit on one side of the origin, the visible signature of a distinct \emph{status-valuation} axis that opposes evaluation to both preference and consumption.

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy Among Complex Taste Aspects}
\label{sec:rv}

Are the three aspects of complex taste redundant or partially independent? The RV coefficients in Table~\ref{tab:rv} support partial independence. Preference and consumption are moderately linked ($RV = 0.32$): people who like a genre are more likely to have listened to it, but the two structures are far from interchangeable. Evaluation, by contrast, is nearly orthogonal to both ($RV = 0.01$ with each), consistent with the idea that evaluative categories are largely shared across ``brow'' levels \citep{jæger2024from-a4b}. This near-orthogonality is the geometric signature of the complex taste idea. Status attributions about who listens to a genre are structurally independent of taste, distinct from preferences and engagement. A respondent's evaluation profile is, to a first approximation, empirically distinct from their preference and consumption profiles. Complex tastes---configurations in which the aspects disagree---are therefore not measurement noise or respondent inconsistency; they are the expected product of applying three distinct criteria of judgment to the same cultural objects.

\subsection{Partial Axes}

We can represent a given aspect's partial axis by correlating its individual scores from the separate analysis with the scores on each global axis (Table~\ref{tab:partial-axes}), which in turn help us interpret the latter. The first dimension of the global space is the axis of maximal consensus for preference and consumption: it correlates strongly with the first axes of their separate MCA analyses ($0.84$ and $0.86$, respectively), while evaluation's leading axis correlates only weakly ($0.19$), matching its modest $2.5\%$ contribution. This suggests that people who like many genres (preference omnivores) are also likely to consume many genres (engagement omnivores), but not necessarily regard many genres highly. The second dimension, which separates genres along a highbrow--popular axis, relates closely to the second axes of both the separate preference ($-0.87$) and consumption ($+0.89$) analyses---genres are separated along similar lines for both aspects---with a modest assist from evaluation's second axis ($+0.35$), matching its $11.0\%$ contribution; this tells us that people tend to organize both their preference and consumption along the ``brow'' levels separating highbrow from popular genres, but this tendency is independent of their evaluation of those genres. By contrast, the third status-valuation dimension of the global space is defined almost exclusively by evaluation, with the leading axis from the separate evaluation MCA correlating at $+0.91$, but the leading axes of the separate preference and consumption MCA not correlated at all with the third global dimension ($-0.16$ and $-0.07$, respectively).

\subsection{Composition of the Dimensions of Complex Taste Space}
\label{sec:contrib}

Table~\ref{tab:groups} reports the quantities that answer the second and third questions posed above: does each aspect actually participate in the global compromise, and which aspect organizes each dimension of the shared space? The answer to the second question is yes: Each aspect contributes to each of the three global dimensions.\footnote{Note that MFA's balancing weights---the inverses of the first eigenvalues of the separate analyses ($5.00$ for preference, $6.45$ for consumption, and $4.28$ for evaluation)---put the three aspects on equal footing; the separate analyses' first eigenvalues are themselves of comparable strength ($0.20$, $0.16$, and $0.23$).} 

To answer the third question, we see that while all aspects appear in the first three global dimensions, none is equally represented in any one dimension. Preference and consumption more or less equally organize the first two dimensions (contributing $48.1\%$ and $49.4\%$ to Dimension 1, and $40.0\%$ and $48.9\%$ to Dimension 2), but the third dimension is different in kind, being mainly organized by evaluation, which contributes $83.9\%$, against $8.0\%$ and $8.1\%$ for the other two. 

The content of the third evaluation-dominant dimension is unambiguous, as \emph{every one} of the twenty evaluation ``yes'' categories lies on the same (positive) side of Dimension 3 (mean coordinate $+1.12$; range $+0.20$ to $+1.87$), while the ``yes'' categories of preference and consumption collapse toward the origin on it (ranges $-0.41$ to $+0.12$ and $-0.59$ to $+0.21$). The evaluation categories are themselves ordered by rarity: granting high status to the fans of rap/hip-hop ($+1.87$), Latin/Spanish/Salsa ($+1.84$), or country ($+1.67$) is the distinctive position, while granting it to the fans of opera ($+0.20$) or classical ($+0.23$) is relatively common, barely differentiating respondents. Dimension 3 is thus a distinct axis organized by \emph{status valuation} rather than preference or engagement.

The $Lg$ coefficients answer the dimension composition question from the other direction, as every aspect leaves a detectable imprint on the compromise---none is present in name only---but unevenly. The link between evaluation and the MFA ($Lg = 1.14$) is weaker than the links of preference ($1.95$) and consumption ($2.48$).


\subsection{Measuring Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

We measure complex tastes geometrically, as the dispersion $W_s(i)$ of an individual's three partial points (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), read directly off the MFA. Ma's eight configurations provide a discrete complement to this measure; we cover them in Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} and borrow their vocabulary throughout.

The three scores differ in what disagreement means, because each inherits its interpretation from its dimension: on the first, the general-affirmation axis, the aspects disagree about how much the respondent chooses genres, a disagreement that runs between liking and listening (evaluation barely separates respondents on that axis); on the second, they disagree about where the respondent sits on the highbrow--popular ladder they all share; on the third, where liking and listening barely register, disagreement means status attributions reaching further down the genre hierarchy than an engagement profile with no position on that axis can accompany.\footnote{Because liking and listening barely vary on the third dimension, $W_3$ behaves partly like a squared position score: it correlates at $0.72$ with the absolute value of the respondent's third-dimension coordinate (against $0.37$ for $W_2$), and its mean rises from $5.7$ among respondents who grant unambiguous high status to none of the twenty genres to $156$ among those who grant it to all twenty. $W_3$ is best read as measuring how far the attribution profile extends beyond what an engagement profile can accompany, not as a count of per-genre contradictions.} On the first three dimensions, the dispersion of partial points accounts for $56\%$, $52\%$, and $63\%$ of the average projected partial inertia, respectively: by geometry alone, disagreement between aspects contributes about as much to respondents' positions as agreement does, itself an argument for the idea of complex tastes. 

On the third dimension, the pair-level decomposition locates the disagreement where theory predicts: the preference--evaluation ($\rho = 0.16$ with the dimension) and consumption--evaluation ($\rho = 0.14$) pairs disagree most---though only weakly---among respondents near the pole anchored by the genre evaluations. The average shares (Table~\ref{tab:pairs}) echo the aspect-independence result of Section~\ref{sec:rv}: on the second dimension, where all three aspects place respondents on a shared ladder, preference and consumption positions correlate at $r = 0.73$, and their pair accounts for only $18\%$ of the average within-person disagreement, against $47\%$ for consumption--evaluation alone; on the third dimension, where liking and listening barely move, the preference--consumption pair all but vanishes ($2\%$). Wherever evaluation varies, it carries the disagreement. The first dimension is the contrast: its disagreement splits almost evenly across the three pairs (a third apiece), so no aspect stands apart on the affirmation axis; there, liking and listening disagree about level of engagement around an evaluation point that barely moves, unlike the second and third dimensions, where evaluation is the aspect that stands apart. Nor are complex tastes concentrated in any region of the space: the aspect-disagreement score on the first dimension is essentially unrelated to positions on the other two ($\rho = 0.01$ and $-0.07$), so high-disagreement respondents are spread across the hierarchical and status-valuation axes rather than clustered anywhere in particular.

An example makes the decomposition easier to grasp (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}). Consider a respondent who likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, Broadway/show tunes, and classic rock/oldies to top 40 and contemporary rock---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status. On the first (horizontal) dimension, the general-affirmation axis, all three aspect points sit on the same side of the origin---preference at $+3.53$, consumption at $+3.05$, evaluation at $+2.28$, around a global point of $+2.95$---so the aspects disagree only about \emph{how much} this respondent engages, and only modestly: $W_1 = 0.8$, or 3\% of the projected partial inertia. The second dimension (right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}), the highbrow--popular hierarchy axis, gives an intermediate case: the aspects disagree not about how much this respondent engages but about where they sit on the ladder. The preference point sits just on the popular side of the origin ($-0.89$), while consumption and evaluation sit on the highbrow side ($+1.74$ and $+4.31$), around a global point of $+1.72$, giving $W_2 = 13.5$---60\% of the projected partial inertia---and here it is liking that stands apart from the other two.\footnote{As the discrete complement to this geometric measure, each genre--respondent pair is classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex tastes (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}).} The third (vertical) dimension, the status-valuation axis, tells a different story: now it is evaluation that stands apart from the other two. The preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.66$ and $-1.33$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the side anchored by the genre evaluations ($+13.12$): this respondent grants high status to nearly every genre's fans, a generosity of valuation that far outruns both their liking and their listening. The global point is $+3.71$, and now the disagreement dwarfs the position: $W_3 = (-0.66 - 3.71)^2 + (-1.33 - 3.71)^2 + (13.12 - 3.71)^2 = 133.1$, or 76\% of the projected partial inertia---nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects, not shared orientation.\footnote{In Ma's combinatorial terms (see Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}), the same respondent holds thirteen genres in complex configurations: one guilty pleasure, seven taste poses, four instances of distant praise, and one instance of distanced consumption.} Applying the genre-level split (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}) sharpens the reading: the respondent's genre-based complex taste sums to only $8.5$ across the twenty genres---the largest single-genre term, a taste pose in Latin/Spanish/Salsa, is just $1.0$---so almost none of the $W_3$ score of $133.1$ is composed of complex tastes based in a particular genre. The remaining $94\%$ reflects cross-genre coherence. Across the eighteen genres whose fans this respondent thinks of as high status, the evaluation aspect pulls away from preference and consumption in the same direction, systematically orienting one aspect against the other two rather than disagreeing about any one genre.

The two measurement approaches also diverge in instructive ways (Table~\ref{tab:antinomy}). The geometric aspect-disagreement score on Dimension 1 tracks the total number of complex tastes ($\rho = 0.31$; $\rho = 0.27$ with total dispersion across the first three dimensions), but its counterparts on Dimensions 2 and 3 do not ($0.19$ and $-0.06$). The lesson is that geometric and combinatorial measures of complex tastes are related but not interchangeable: the dispersion of partial points captures \emph{how much} the aspects disagree overall, while the configuration counts capture \emph{which genres} the disagreement attaches to. They align where complex tastes are a matter of degree of engagement (Dimension 1) and diverge where they are a matter of hierarchical placement (Dimensions 2 and 3).

The genre-level decomposition (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}) shows what these scores are made of, and most of it is coherence rather than genre-based complex taste. Averaged over respondents, genre-based complex taste accounts for only $29\%$ of $W_1$, $48\%$ of $W_2$, and $23\%$ of $W_3$: the typical respondent's aspect disagreement is a repeated pattern---valuation or engagement consistently outrunning the other aspects---rather than a set of genre-based complex tastes. The genre-based component is also the part of the score that carries the combinatorial signal: it correlates with the total number of complex configurations at $\rho = 0.71$ and $0.66$ on Dimensions 1 and 2 (Table~\ref{tab:antinomy}) (against $0.31$ and $0.19$ for the scores themselves), while the coherence component has no combinatorial counterpart at all. The two components can also pull apart within a single respondent: 196 respondents ($9\%$ of the sample) sit in the bottom third of $W_3$ but the top third of its genre-based component, holding complex tastes concentrated in specific genres that cancel against each other in the global score---complexity the aggregate measure does not register.

The configuration counts have their own geometric signatures, which is what makes them interpretable in the space. Distant praise sits squarely on the status-valuation dimension ($\rho = +0.79$, the pole anchored by the genre evaluations): it concentrates in consecrated genres whose fans' status respondents grant without liking or consuming them---the survey analogue of the unread bestseller. Guilty pleasures lean toward the popular pole of Dimension 2 ($\rho = -0.25$) and sit at the opposite, status-withholding pole of Dimension 3 ($\rho = -0.24$), joined there by justified abstentions ($\rho = -0.33$). Taste poses show up among respondents high on the general-affirmation dimension ($\rho = 0.22$) who lean toward both the highbrow pole ($\rho = 0.34$) and the status-granting pole of Dimension 3 ($\rho = 0.37$). The genre-based columns of Table~\ref{tab:antinomy} draw the same map for the genre-based component of the score: guilty pleasures carry genre-based disagreement on the first two dimensions ($\rho = 0.53$ and $0.43$ with $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$), taste poses ($0.47$) and distant praise ($0.38$) on the third, and simple non-tastes sit uniformly low ($-0.75$ on the first two); even simple tastes retain some genre-based disagreement on the status-valuation dimension ($0.57$), a residue of the aspects' differing margins rather than of complex taste.

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

To situate the sources of complex tastes socially, we project a set of respondent demographics---gender, race/ethnicity, age, education, parental education, household income, subjective social class, and census region---as supplementary variables onto the MFA representation. Supplementary variables don't influence the analysis: a category's coordinates are the barycenter of its members' positions in the common space, and how strongly each variable associates with each dimension is summarized by the correlation ratio $\eta^2$ (Tables~\ref{tab:eta} and \ref{tab:sup-coord}; Figure~\ref{fig:supplementary}).

The social anatomy of the taste space runs mainly through the highbrow--popular dimension. Age is the strongest single anchor ($\eta^2 = 0.33$), with a nearly monotone gradient: respondents aged 18--29 sit at $-0.74$ on Dimension 2, those 30--39 at $-0.41$, those 40--49 at $-0.18$, those 50--59 at $+0.19$, those 60--69 at $+0.71$, and those 70 and older at $+1.23$---the genre hierarchy doubles as an age hierarchy. Education traces the same axis monotonically (No diploma $-0.26$, HS/GED $-0.25$, some college $-0.11$, Associate's degree $-0.09$, BA $+0.09$, MA $+0.51$, professional or doctoral degree $+0.67$; $\eta^2 = 0.05$), as does subjective social class (Lower $-0.35$, Working $-0.23$, Middle $+0.24$, Upper $+0.39$; $\eta^2 = 0.06$), with household income and race/ethnicity following more weakly (income from $-0.16$ to $+0.19$; Hispanic $-0.42$, Black $-0.26$, White $+0.16$). Gender and census region are negligible across all four dimensions.

The general-affirmation dimension is only weakly socially structured---no demographic variable exceeds $\eta^2 = 0.03$ on it---but the education pattern is instructive: the gradient concentrates at the bottom of the credential distribution (No diploma $-0.39$, HS/GED $-0.24$) and flattens from some college upward ($+0.05$ to $+0.13$). Generalized engagement with the genre system, in other words, is most sharply differentiated at the entry into credentials, not across their full range.

The status-valuation dimension, by contrast, is strikingly \emph{socially flat}. No demographic variable exceeds $\eta^2 = 0.011$ on it, and every category barycenter lies within about $\pm 0.2$ of the origin (Table~\ref{tab:sup-coord}). Whatever divides respondents on this dimension---the propensity to grant unambiguous high status to some genres' fans rather than others---isn't captured by the standard stratification variables. This fits the dimension's near-perfect geometric independence from preference and consumption established above, and it sharpens how we should read the status-valuation axis: not a credential or class gradient in disguise, but a structuring of taste whose social sources lie outside the standard demographic inventory.

The fourth dimension is a different case. It's carried almost entirely by liking and listening (engagement contributes 57\% of its inertia and preference 37\%, against 6\% for evaluation), and it's the only dimension besides the highbrow--popular axis with a strong demographic anchor. Race/ethnicity stands out ($\eta^2 = 0.26$; no other variable exceeds $0.03$): Black respondents sit far toward its positive pole ($+0.98$), followed by Hispanic ($+0.34$) and multiple-race ($+0.33$) respondents, while White respondents sit at $-0.30$ (Table~\ref{tab:sup-coord}). The category coordinates show what this gradient tracks (Figure~\ref{fig:dim4}). Engagement with reggae ($+0.77$), Latin/Spanish/Salsa ($+0.67$), rap/hip-hop ($+0.52$), and Blues/R\&B ($+0.45$) defines the positive pole, mirrored in preference (rap/hip-hop $+0.50$, Latin/Spanish/Salsa $+0.47$); engagement with heavy metal ($-0.74$), indie and alternative rock ($-0.62$), contemporary rock ($-0.61$), classic rock/oldies ($-0.45$), and, more moderately, country, bluegrass, and folk ($-0.31$ to $-0.36$) defines the negative pole. Evaluation, by contrast, barely spreads along this dimension (most categories within $\pm 0.2$ of the origin). The two poles cut across the highbrow--popular hierarchy---rap/hip-hop and heavy metal sit on the same side of Dimension 2 but opposite poles of Dimension 4---so the dimension records a racialized segmentation of engagement, Black-rooted genres against the rock--country cluster, rather than a repeat of the canonical-hierarchy contrast. Combined with the social flatness of the status-valuation dimension, the pattern is pointed: where respondents' likes and listening divide sharply along racialized genre lines, what they're willing to praise does not.

\subsection{Who Has Complex Tastes?}
\label{sec:who}

Measuring complex tastes geometrically has one further advantage: $W_s(i)$ is a continuous, dimension-specific quantity, so it can serve directly as the outcome of a standard regression model---something the combinatorial count, a single coarse integer, can't do. Table~\ref{tab:regression} reports OLS regressions of the three aspect-disagreement scores on the same demographics projected as supplementary variables above. The headline result is how small the associations are: the full set of eight demographics accounts for $5.2\%$ of the variance in $W_1$, $2.0\%$ in $W_2$, and $2.1\%$ in $W_3$. Where respondents sit in the taste space is strongly socially patterned (Section~\ref{sec:social}); how much their aspects disagree is nearly socially unstructured. Complex tastes, on the geometric measure, are spread across the social structure rather than concentrated in any one segment of it.

The partial effects that do emerge are informative. Disagreement over engagement ($W_1$) is higher among respondents whose parents hold a BA ($+1.32$), among those who identify as more than one race ($+2.51$), and among those who identify as upper class ($+3.67$), and it declines with age ($-1.09$ at ages 30--39 through $-2.09$ at 70+, relative to the youngest cohort): aspect disagreement over liking, listening, and valuing is, if anything, concentrated among the advantaged rather than the excluded. Disagreement over the genre hierarchy ($W_2$) is nearly unpatterned: the only significant coefficient is a modestly higher score among the oldest cohort ($+0.63$). Disagreement over status valuation ($W_3$) is concentrated at the top of the class ladder ($+7.70$ for upper-class identifiers) and rises with age ($+2.04$ to $+2.73$ across the adult cohorts), with Hispanic respondents higher ($+1.89$) and those with an Associate's degree lower ($-3.79$) than their reference categories.

These findings hold up under a logarithmic transformation of the outcomes, which addresses the skew in the $W$ scores: the parental-education effect on $W_1$ persists (partial $F = 5.2$), as does the subjective-class effect ($F = 2.3$; the upper-class premium is $+0.40$ on the log scale), and a gender difference emerges on the log scale, with women showing lower $W_1$ ($F = 11.8$); the subjective-class effect on $W_3$ also persists ($F = 2.7$). The same demographics also predict the pairwise disagreement components of Dimension 3, and tell a consistent story: upper-class identification raises both preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation disagreement (partial $F = 3.9$ and $4.9$), while preference--consumption disagreement is patterned mainly by parental education and subjective class ($F = 15.2$ and $9.3$). At the individual level, then, complex tastes aren't the signature of any particular social location; they arise wherever the three weakly coupled measurement systems happen to diverge.

Because the aspect-disagreement scores blend genre-based complex tastes with the cross-genre orientation of one aspect against the other two (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}), we also estimated the models with the genre-based component---the $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ term of Equation~\ref{eq:genre}, the respondent's genre-based complex taste---as the outcome. The conclusions hold, and the patterning is somewhat stronger: the demographics account for $8.5\%$, $8.0\%$, and $3.3\%$ of the variance in the genre-based components of $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_3$ (against $5.2\%$, $2.0\%$, and $2.1\%$ for the full scores). The upper-class premium appears on all three dimensions ($+0.25$, $+0.25$, and $+0.58$, all $p < 0.01$)---including the hierarchy dimension, where the full score shows none---and parental education still raises genre-based disagreement over engagement and the genre hierarchy ($+0.10$ and $+0.11$, both $p < 0.001$). The age effects are where the two components part ways. On the status-valuation dimension, genre-based complex taste rises with age just as the full score does ($+0.24$ to $+0.48$). On the hierarchy dimension, they decline across every cohort ($-0.08$ to $-0.28$) even as the full score shows the oldest cohort higher ($+0.63$): the oldest respondents' higher $W_2$ comes from the cross-genre coherence component, not from complex tastes tied to particular genres.

Equation~\ref{eq:genre} is an exact identity, so the full-score coefficients decompose additively as well: each demographic's coefficient on $W_s$ is the sum of its coefficients on the two components. That split is one-sided. The upper-class premium on the status-valuation dimension sits almost entirely in the coherence component ($+7.12$ of the $+7.70$), and the age coefficients land there too ($+1.37$ to $+2.25$, with the two oldest cohorts significant); on the affirmation dimension, the upper-class ($+3.42$ of $+3.67$) and parental-education ($+1.23$ of $+1.32$) premiums are likewise almost all coherence. Partly this is scale---the genre-based component averages only $29\%$, $48\%$, and $23\%$ of the scores---but the asymmetry has a reading in the terms of the decomposition itself. Genre-based complex taste is disagreement bound to particular genres, a set of local accommodations to specific objects; coherence is one aspect standing off from the other two in the same direction across the whole portfolio---a transposable, disposition-like orientation rather than a set of genre-specific configurations (negative coherence, by contrast, means genre-based complex tastes that point in opposite directions across genres and cancel). Social location, in other words, tracks the transposable part: what demographic advantage buys is not so much a portfolio of complex tastes bound to particular genres as a systematic orientation of one aspect against the other two, repeated wherever one looks. This is also a distinction the geometric approach can measure and the combinatorial one cannot. Ma's configurations are nominal types: the same configuration can of course recur---the same distant praise in genre after genre---but a configuration carries no magnitude and no direction, so recurrent configurations can neither accumulate into a total disagreement nor cancel one another; without that arithmetic, the question of how much of a person's disagreement is a transposable orientation and how much is bound to particular genres has no combinatorial answer.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure: individuals are \emph{sources} of complex tastes, and genres are \emph{targets}. To measure the target side, we transpose the analysis: individuals are now the twenty genres, and each aspect block contains one binary variable per respondent---whether that respondent likes, listens to, or grants unambiguous high status to the genre. Respondents whose answers are constant across all twenty genres within an aspect (who like nothing, listen to nothing, or are constant in their status attributions) define variables with an empty category and contribute no genre discrimination, so they're dropped (83, 84, and 326 respondent-variables respectively). The transposition is not a mere rearrangement of the original solution. In simple correspondence analysis, the row and column clouds are dual, so genre coordinates could be read off the original fit at no cost; but multiple correspondence analysis with a block structure breaks that duality. The original analysis's category coordinates locate a genre through the composition of its audience---the barycenter of the respondents who affirm it---while the transposed analysis locates genres as objects, with distances computed over the respondent-indicators within each aspect block. Because MFA weights each block by the inverse of its separate analysis's first eigenvalue, and transposing changes the separate analyses, the balancing weights and hence the eigen-decomposition differ: the transposed dimensions are optimized for the dispersion of the genre cloud rather than the respondent cloud ($\lambda_1 = 2.27$ here against $1.51$ above). And statistics defined over the individuals of an analysis---RV coefficients and partial points among them---don't survive transposition: the genre-level RV coefficients and aspect-specific genre partial points reported below exist only in the transposed fit. The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level \textsf{FactoMineR} solution: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions all agree to within $10^{-4}$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA. Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map}
\end{figure}

The central result of the duality analysis is that, from the object side, the aspects \emph{agree}. The genre-level RV coefficients are $0.92$ (preference--consumption), $0.53$ (preference--evaluation), and $0.49$ (consumption--evaluation)---against $0.32$, $0.01$, and $0.01$ at the individual level. The disagreement that constitutes complex tastes is therefore not a property of the objects: the population that likes a genre, the population that listens to it, and the population that credits its fans with high status overlap substantially---far more than the corresponding individual-level profiles coincide. What varies, and what generates complex tastes, is whether a given individual occupies all three positions toward a given genre at once. Aspect independence is an individual-level achievement, not a genre-level partition.

\label{tab:genre-profile}

\end{table}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.27$, $14.6\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.95$, $12.5\%$). Its second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}). At the positive pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = +0.77$), as taste poses ($+0.55$), as guilty pleasures ($+0.44$), or as justified abstentions ($+0.44$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($+3.7$), mood/easy listening ($+2.0$), country ($+1.8$), and top 40/pop ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit genres whose dominant relation is simple non-taste ($\rho = -0.73$): rap/hip-hop ($-1.7$), reggae ($-1.5$), Latin/Spanish/Salsa ($-1.3$), and heavy metal ($-1.3$)---together with opera ($-1.2$), whose relation to its audience is instead dominated by distant praise ($58.9\%$ of respondents hold it in that configuration). The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way complex-taste theory anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera). The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($-3.6$), opera ($-3.0$), and Broadway/show tunes ($-2.1$), with distant-praise rates loading at $-0.82$ and taste-pose rates at $-0.58$---against genres held in guilty pleasure ($\rho = +0.75$) and distanced consumption ($+0.80$): top 40 ($+2.0$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.8$), classic rock/oldies ($+1.3$), and contemporary rock ($+1.3$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement.

Finally, the partial points show where the aspects disagree about specific objects despite their overall agreement. On the third dimension, the evaluation partial points of consecrated genres sit displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.3$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and $+0.9$ for consumption; opera: $+2.3$ against $-0.0$ and $+0.1$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-0.8$ against $-3.1$ and $-4.1$). Status attributions, in other words, are distributed across genres in a way that only partially tracks who likes and who listens---echoing, at the level of objects, the aspect independence we already established at the level of sources.

\section{Discussion}

[DRAFT: The results establish three things. First, the three aspects of taste are empirically distinct structures, with evaluation nearly orthogonal to preference and consumption. Second, the shared space of taste is organized by a general-engagement gradient and a highbrow--popular hierarchy, both of which are visible in all aspects. Third, there exists a third-order dimension driven disproportionately by status evaluation---a candidate geometric locus for complex tastes. The operationalization of complex tastes is carried out in Section~\ref{sec:antinomies}, their social sources in Section~\ref{sec:social}, their individual-level correlates in Section~\ref{sec:who}, and the duality of sources and targets in Section~\ref{sec:duality}. The remaining steps are full introductory and discussion prose.]

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm of this taste culture, not the exception. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't credit that way. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration.
